alignment.note: Greek opens with the Septuagintalism καὶ ἐγένετο ('and it came to pass') followed by an articular infinitive of time; the Peshitta and Vulgate both compress this into a simple temporal conjunction (ܘܟܕ / Et dum, 'and while'), eliminating the Hebraising 'it came to pass' auxiliary verb.

The Greek articular-infinitive temporal clause ἐν τῷ σπείρειν ('in the sowing') is rendered by both versions with a finite verb governed by the conjunction above: Syriac ܙܪܥ and Latin seminat, a present-tense indicative. The Vulgate notably omits any expressed subject, leaving 'the sower' implicit as in the Greek.

Greek uses the partitive correlative ὃ μέν ('the one part'), anticipating later δέ clauses; the Vulgate renders this with the indefinite aliud ('another part'), while the Peshitta employs the existential particle ܐܝܬ plus a relative ܕܢܦܠ ('there is [seed] which fell'), a periphrastic construction idiomatic to Syriac narrative.

Greek παρὰ τὴν ὁδόν ('alongside the road') and Latin circa viam align closely; the Peshitta adds the noun ܝܕ (literally 'hand/side') before ܐܘܪܚܐ, forming the idiomatic ܥܠ ܝܕ ܐܘܪܚܐ ('upon the side of the road'), a typical Syriac periphrastic preposition with no separate equivalent in the other traditions.

Greek ἦλθεν is singular (agreeing with neuter plural subject τὰ πετεινά per the Attic rule), whereas the Vulgate venerunt is plural; the Peshitta ܘܐܬܬ is feminine singular, agreeing with its grammatically feminine subject ܦܪܚܬܐ, here treated as a collective.

Greek τὰ πετεινὰ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ and Latin volucres cæli both preserve the qualifier 'of heaven'; the Peshitta has only the bare collective singular ܦܪܚܬܐ ('the bird[s]/fowl'), omitting the genitive 'of heaven' and using a collective for the Greek/Latin plural.

Greek κατέφαγεν αὐτό and Latin comederunt illud express the verb and its object as separate words; the Peshitta ܘܐܟܠܬܗ fuses the conjunction, the verb 'ate', and the enclitic 3ms object suffix into a single inflected form, a feature of Syriac verbal morphology, and again carries singular agreement with the collective subject.
